Site Plan Application #26-009 – Amended and Restated Eighth Amendment to Hartland Towne Square Planned Development Agreement Director Langer stated the following:  Gave an overview of the location and scope of the Hartland Towne Square Planned Development.  Developed as a PD Planned Development.  Pattern Book established specific regulations for this development which can vary from the Zoning Ordinance.  Amending those regulations involves a recommendation by the Planning Commission, and final approval from the Township Board.  This is the 8th Amendment restated; there was an 8th Amendment approved earlier by the Township and the HTS owners at that time, RAMCO, but Meijer would not sign the document.  This document includes those changes and some additional items. The Applicant, Steve Samona, representing Hartland Towne Square LLC, introduced himself and stated the following:  Purchased the property at the end of 2025 trying to breathe new life into the development.  They view Hartland as a thriving community with momentum. 2 HARTLAND TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION DRAFT MEETING MINUTES SEPTEMBER 24, 2026 – 7:00 PM   Have a desire to see this development succeed; they felt the need to modernize the Pattern Book to draw more interest and remove some items that may have been hampering projects from achieving success in the past. Applicant submitted the following items: o Exhibit A: “Land” o Exbibit B: “Purchased Property” o Exhibit C: “Existing Development Sign Improvements” o Exhibit D: “New Ground Signs’ o Exhibit E: “New Development Signs” o Exhibit F: “LED Lights” o Exhibit G: “Landscape Modifications” o Exhibit H: “Current Site Plan” o Exhibit I: “New Sign Map” Chair Fox referred to the staff memorandum dated September 17, 2026. Paragraph 6.2 of the Agreement (Internal Traffic Circulation) – (#2 and #3 on Page 2 of the Agreement) Director Langer stated the following:  Hartland Road was reconfigured when Hartland Towne Square was planned and bisects a portion of the development.  Two private roads, Hartland Towne Square and Rovey Drive, are also part of the PD.  Land divisions occurred, whereby the right-of-way area for Hartland Square Drive and Rovey Drive appeared to be exempted from the ownership of the adjacent parcel(s).  This presented potential future concerns with the ownership and maintenance of both Hartland Square Drive and Rovey Drive and was discussed in 2019.  The 8th Amendment of 2019 provided proposed language to address this concern and is included in this amendment. Paragraph 3.1.16 of the Agreement (Drive Through Service) – (#4 on Page 2 & #5 on Page 3 of the Agreement) Director Langer stated the following:  Previously, there was a cap on the number of drive-throughs for businesses and restaurants.  After COVID, the restaurant industry changed and more drive-throughs were desired.  The 8th Amendment from 2019 provided language to eliminate the restrictions on the number of drive-through establishments and the new owners have carried this forward. Sign Program Overview for Monument/Ground Signs Chair Fox stated the following:  Indicated on their plans the signs they would like to have with red circles and have stated the reasons for them.  Exposure to Highland Road is limited; the Applicant feels additional signage would help drive customer traffic to those sites.  Commented this development could be forty percent (40%) of the retail space in Hartland Township. Hartland Township Page 2 Updated 10/1/26 3 HARTLAND TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION DRAFT MEETING MINUTES SEPTEMBER 24, 2026 – 7:00 PM Commissioner Eckman stated he supports the additional signage given the size of the parcel(s). He appreciates signage when he is navigating in an unfamiliar area. Commissioner Grissim asked about sign number four (4) listed as Exhibit C. Chair Fox reminded the Planning Commission of an earlier discussion about a sign near the Starbuck’s multi-unit building. Director Langer stated that sixteen-foot sign was proposed in the original 8th Amendment and was never constructed; the Applicant is proposing a new sign with multiple panels. LED Lights (Exhibit F) – (#9 on Page 4 of the Agreement) Chair Fox stated this change updates the Pattern Book with the new LED lighting options that many projects have used recently. Landscape Modifications (Exhibit G) – (#10 on Page 4 of the Agreement) Commissioner Grissim stated she visited the site; the evergreen trees that will be replaced have grown into the other trees. They intend to replace the older evergreen trees with a different variety that will be six feet (6’) in height and will screen the parking areas; all the Landscaping Modifications are acceptable. Commissioner Eckman inquired if this type of evergreen will stop growing at six feet (6’) to avoid this issue in the future. Commissioner Grissim confirmed it is a salt tolerant, shrub-type of evergreen. Paragraph 3 of the Agreement (Permitted Uses, Limitations, and Prohibited Uses) – (#12-#16 on Pages 4 &5 of the Agreement) Director Langer stated they are modifying the original list of uses and limitations, in particular, a gas station. The original plan allowed for a gas station on the Meijer property but nowhere else. Meijer is interested in a different location for their gas station. This change would permit them to pursue another location within the development. Chair Fox continued the original uses were proposed by the developer and accepted by the Township; the proposed uses seem reasonable. The Applicant stated they are trying to adapt to the ongoing changes in retail. Modifications to the Façade Materials on Buildings – (#17 & #18 on Page 5 of the Agreement) Director Langer stated the following:  Larger uses have a quick brick component which has improved over the last twenty years.  Allowing this component on buildings larger than 5,000 square feet.  Those buildings still must come before the Planning Commission for Site Plan Approval. Maximum Building Height – (#19 on Page 5 of the Agreement) Director Langer stated the building height limitation was put in place due to the limitation of the fire fighting equipment at that time; that has changed so they are asking to increase the height limitation. The Planning Commission briefly discussed the new height limitation and the process for approval. Hartland Township Page 3 Updated 10/1/26 4 HARTLAND TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION DRAFT MEETING MINUTES SEPTEMBER 24, 2026 – 7:00 PM Wall Signs Director Langer stated the following:  Not part of the PD Agreement.  Asked the Applicant to provide a chart to aid the Planning Commission in understanding the changes.  Requesting more signage, larger signs, and multiple signs for larger tenants. Chair Fox stated the Applicant also provided examples of larger buildings with the requested signage, and they looked about right. The Applicant offered some additional explanation. The Planning Commission discussed the changes. Delivery of products, goods or merchandise – (#26 on Page 7 of the Agreement) Chair Fox explained there were some limitations in the original PD, this change will open this up. The Planning Commission discussed truck idling and a past concern at Meijer around Thanksgiving. Amendment to Previously Approved Landscape Plans – Approval Procedure Director Langer stated this is a separate request, a Site Plan Amendment. It consists of a revised landscape plan for the roundabout and clock tower, Exhibit L-1.C. Commissioner Grissim asked about the purpose. The Applicant stated it looked a little neglected and they intend to beautify the area with fresh landscaping. The Planning Commission discussed the timing, the process and what has already been done. Commissioner Mitchell offered the following Motion: Move to recommend approval of Site Plan Application #26-009, for the Amended and Restated Eighth Amendment to Hartland Towne Square Planned Development Agreement, as outlined in the staff memorandum dated September 17, 2026. The recommendation for approval is based on the following findings: 1. The Planning Commission has determined the proposed amendment provides clarification for the on-going maintenance of the private roads in the development. 2. The Planning Commission has determined the proposed amendment to remove the limitation on the number of drive-through establishments, provides flexibility for existing and future businesses in the development. 3. The Planning Commission has determined the proposed amendments to allow additional ground signs, make improvements to existing ground signs, and amend the wall sign standards improves the visibility for existing and future businesses in the development. 4. The Planning Commission has determined the amendment to update the lighting standards to add LED light pole heads will be a benefit to the PD and the Township. OLD BUSINESS (PC-10-26) (OR206-26) Map Amendment (Rezoning) (PC-10-26) (OR-206-26) Map Amendment (Rezoning) Lynn Wilson Presented a petition to amend the zoning map that has been submitted by Nathan Waggner. The applicant is requesting approval to rezone 47.24 acres from Single Family Residential (R-1) to Multiple Family Residential (MF). The subject property is located at S. Scott Rd and Wildcat Rd., Section 15 of Bingham Township (Parcel ID: 030-015-200-010-50). Page | 4 Miles Roblyer addressed questions about the rezoning process, noting that planning and zoning procedures are highly specialized and often unfamiliar to residents until a project gains attention. He explained that the process is governed by the Michigan Zoning Enabling Act, and that a rezoning must occur before any site plan can be considered. He acknowledged public frustration but clarified that the Commission is required to follow the state-mandated sequence, which is why the rezoning is being addressed at this stage. Todd Krajniare, representing the developer, provided an overview of the development history and efforts undertaken over several years to identify feasible housing options for the community. He explained challenges related to infrastructure, particularly water and sewer capacity, and noted that single-family housing is not economically viable given current construction costs and local income levels. He described outreach to multiple builders and developers and stated that multi-family development was the only option that met market demand and affordability needs. He outlined the developer’s background, experience in small communities, and commitment to market-rate housing without subsidies. He also detailed the site selection process and explained why alternative locations were not viable due to zoning, land availability, and infrastructure constraints. He concluded that the proposed site meets planning criteria and provides an appropriate transition between nearby commercial, industrial, and residential uses. Nathan Waggner introduced himself as the engineer of record and addressed several technical aspects of the proposal. He noted that letters from the Board of Public Works indicate adequate utility capacity for the project. He stated that multi-family development generates less traffic per unit than single-family housing and that preliminary estimates show approximately one additional vehicle per minute during peak periods. He addressed drainage concerns, explaining that multi-family development can reduce impervious surface areas compared to single-family layouts and that all stormwater would be managed on site. He referenced studies indicating that adjacent property values are not negatively impacted by apartment developments. He discussed potential setbacks and buffering options, noting these will be addressed in detail at the site plan stage. He concluded by responding to questions regarding site layout, market conditions, and local housing needs. The Commission reviewed the required findings of facts related to the rezoning petition. Staff clarified that no identifiable conditions have changed to justify the amendment other than the applicant’s request. It was also stated that no administrative error occurred in the original Page | 5 zoning ordinance. An example was provided from a previous case where a GIS parcel number error required correction through rezoning. Commissioners discussed precedent, noting concerns about consistency between rural and urban areas and the importance of relying on the currently adopted Future Land Use Map, while noting the importance of the upcoming Comprehensive Plan update. Staff confirmed that utility providers indicated adequate public services, with traffic impacts to be addressed during any future development review. Commissioners considered whether the rezoning would affect environmental conditions, including nearby regulated wetlands and soil limitations, but noted these issues would be evaluated more specifically at the site plan stage. Staff reiterated that the findings must focus on the rezoning itself and potential uses within the MF district, independent of any particular development proposal. The Commission also confirmed that the request aligns with the adopted Future Land Use Map. Potential environmental impacts such as wastewater, drainage, and soil characteristics were discussed, with recognition that detailed analysis would occur during site plan review. The Clinton County Board of Commissioners Page 2 of 16 Future Land Use Map: recognizes that the exercise of zoning authority under MCL 125.3201(1) and (3) is an empowerment of the Board to plan and zone for a broad range of purposes. It defines the fundamental structure of a zoning ordinance by requiring a zoning plan to consider the interests of the entire community and to ensure that a broad range of land uses is permitted within that community. These provisions empower communities to plan for and regulate a broad array of land uses, taking into consideration the full range of planning concerns that affect the public health, safety, priorities and welfare of the community. Per the 2022 Clinton County Comprehensive Plan Update, the future land use designation is Agricultural Preservation (pp. 29). AGRICULTURAL PRESERVATION Areas designated on the Future Land Use Map as Agricultural Preservation (shown as the color green) are intended to identify areas of prime agricultural land used for production agriculture, small farms, low-density (large lot) residential, agricultural related businesses and industry in order to ensure the conservation of agricultural resource lands of long-term commercial significance for existing and future generations. Additionally, these lands should be protected from interference by adjacent uses which may affect the continued use of these lands for production of food and agricultural products. RURAL-TRANSITIONAL The Rural-Transitional land use designation (shown as the color white) describes various non-urban locations in the County where there is some existing low density residential development along County roadways and land is not suitable (due to topography, soils, vegetation, etc.) for agricultural purposes. The Rural Transitional land use designation provides a transition from prime agricultural land, identified as Agricultural Preservation, to Rural- Low Density Residential. Minimum lot size in the Rural-Transitional land use designation is five (5) acres.
